newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. med students learn about "living with dying".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. med students learn about "living with dying".

text.p: Marilyn Stephens is a wife, mother, church-goer and artist. At 54, she is facing death from cancer.

In the 15 years since the first terrifying lump and the mastectomy, no doctor has ever asked her what she fears. No doctor has ever talked to her about what it will be like as she nears the end of her life. No doctor has ever asked her what help she will need after the chemo stops.

"I am approaching the point where there are no more treatment options for me," she told a lecture hall filled with fresh-faced medical students mesmerised by her story a few days ago. "I know nothing about so many things that I need to know: They keep asking me if I will want to be on a respirator. But what is a respirator? I still don't know."

In their second year of med school, most of these students have not yet ventured into hospital wards. But unlike their counterparts at most medical schools, and unlike generations of doctors before them, future physicians at George Washington University are being taught from the outset that medicine is not just about helping patients live good lives.
It is also about helping them die good deaths.

"You are partners in the patients' living. You are also partners in their dying," said Dr. Christina Puchalski, a resident in internal medicine who has helped take care of Marilyn Stephens and who helped design this unusual class.
DEATH NO LONGER QUICK
Once, death came quickly. Now, people live longer with disease, with pain, with the knowledge that life is ending.

In a landmark study published in 1995, Dr. Joanne Lynn of George Washington University's Centre to Improve Care of the Dying found that too many people were dying alone, in pain, and tethered to machines that were not prolonging their life so much as extending their death.

Among ethicists and physicians, Lynn's study has been something of a watershed, resonating as society's debate over doctor-assisted suicide has come to the fore in the United States and other nations. Two assisted-suicide cases are pending in the U.S. Supreme Court.
Advocates of doctor-assisted suicide believe mentally competent, terminally ill people have the right to decide when enough is enough, when death would be a relief from a life that has become burden.
Critics say calls for assisted suicide would largely disappear if doctors and the health establishment in general learn to tend to the physical and emotional pain of the dying.

Some medical schools, George Washington among them, are beginning to incorporate end-of-life care into the curriculum, not just for advanced students specialising in cancer or geriatrics but for all students early in their careers.

"Until 3 to 5 years ago there was practically nothing taught in medical schools in a systematic way -- a lecture here or there or an elective (course), but nothing was integrated into what medical students were learning about," said Karen Kaplan, director of Choice in Dying, a 50-year-old nonprofit group that is working with a dozen med schools on end-of-life training.
ROLE PLAYING

After Marilyn Stephens spoke to the GW students, they broke into small groups for role-playing exercises, which left them near tears with grief and frustration. One objective was to make the students realise that they must still have something to offer a patient once they can no longer hold out a cure, an idea that seemed almost counter-intuitive for young men and women being instructed in the miracles of 21st century high-tech medicine.

After informing a "patient" that her chemotherapy had failed, student Sunita Bhamidipaty formed a "T" with her hands and looked at her teacher, Dr. Benjamin Blatt, for guidance. "Time-out," she said. "Will I still be her doctor?"
Blatt smiled. Bhamidipaty had grasped the essential question. She would still be the doctor.

"What do you do when there's nothing to offer? Everyone feels like running. The doctor feels, 'I've basically failed,'" Blatt told the class. Then he listed what they could still do -- controlling the woman's pain, prescribing something to help her sleep, helping her plan for her truncated future, just "being with the patient."

When the class was over, the students lingered. Energised by their emotions and their enthusiasm, Christina Puchalski watched for a moment from the hallway. Before returning to her patients in the hospital ward, she made a note to herself -- a promise to call Marilyn Stephens at home that night.
She wanted to make dinner plans. And she wanted to explain what a respirator was.
